first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent me this, so I read it properly, top to bottom. The first paragraph is one very long legal sentence and I had to read it twice on the iPad. Once I got past it, it is clear and sensible, and I like that it points to the government's own pages. It is really written for the two of them, not for me, but the bit about marrying overseas is exactly what I wanted to understand.

journey.quote: In Australia, a celebrant who is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination must say the monitum in section 46(1) of the Marriage Act 1961, which opens "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law", or words to that effect, before you are married.
journey.reaction: That is one sentence with a section number, a quotation and a Latin-sounding word in it. I got there, but it is heavy going as the very first thing I read.

journey.section: What the law requires in an Australian wedding ceremony
journey.quote: General information as at November 2026, not legal advice.
journey.reaction: Good. They are not pretending to be lawyers, and they link to the Attorney-General's Department. That is the sort of honesty I want. Though by the fifth time it appears I had stopped noticing it.

journey.section: The Australian wedding ceremony script, word for word
journey.quote: Celebrant: "Good afternoon, and welcome. [Name] and [Name] have asked you here because you have shaped the people they are, and they want you beside them as they marry."
journey.reaction: That is a lovely line for the families. Not twee, not trendy. I would be happy hearing that.

journey.section: The Australian wedding ceremony script, word for word
journey.quote: **Legally required.** On the day, 3 marriage certificates must be signed by the two of you, your authorised celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18.
journey.reaction: Clear labels on what is required and what is optional. I can follow that, and so can my husband.

journey.section: Witnesses, the signing and the paperwork on the day
journey.quote: Choose two people who will stand close by throughout, not anyone with a job to do.
journey.reaction: Practical. I would have put my brother down as witness and given him the rings as well. Good to know. It made me wonder whether my mother could be a witness and how she would manage standing at a signing table, but it does not say.

journey.section: Witnesses, the signing and the paperwork on the day
journey.quote: Errors on the certificates can be corrected only while the two of you and your witnesses are still present; once the marriage is registered, only the registry's authorised officer can correct them.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of thing nobody tells you. I will make sure someone checks the spelling of the names.

journey.section: Marrying overseas or holding a symbolic ceremony
journey.quote: An Australian script does not carry across borders.
journey.reaction: This is what I actually needed. They are talking about Italy, and I did not know our celebrant could not do it over there.

journey.section: Marrying overseas or holding a symbolic ceremony
journey.quote: That leaves two routes: marry under the destination's own law, or marry legally in Australia with the short script above and hold a symbolic ceremony abroad.
journey.reaction: Marrying under another country's law worries me: paperwork in another language, and who checks it? The page sends me to another article rather than telling me who is responsible.

journey.section: Marrying overseas or holding a symbolic ceremony
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments anywhere in the world as your single point of contact from start to finish, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Now we are talking. One person, and the fee in writing before anything starts. That is what I want to hear when we are paying. But it says 'payments' and does not say what happens to a deposit if an overseas supplier lets us down.

journey.section: Plan the day around the words
journey.quote: When the ceremony is set, your Wedded Advisor works in your time zone, quotes in AUD and confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Quotes in Australian dollars and things in writing. Good. I still do not know who this Advisor is or whether I can speak to them on the phone before anything is booked.

unanswered_questions: Is the deposit protected if an overseas venue or supplier lets us down?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong on the day overseas, at 2am their time?
Can I speak to a real person on the phone before anything is booked, and who would that be?
Does the Advisor help with older relatives travelling, for example my mother who uses a walking frame?
If the children marry under the destination's own law, who makes sure the overseas paperwork is right? (The page rightly says that is not the Advisor's job, but it does not say who.)
Are overseas contracts explained in English, or are we signing in Italian?
Does 'start the conversation' cost anything, and is it a form or a call?

turn_offs_found.quote: In Australia, a celebrant who is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination must say the monitum in section 46(1) of the Marriage Act 1961, which opens "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law", or words to that effect, before you are married.
turn_offs_found.why: A long, unbroken legal sentence as the very first thing on the page. I read carefully, but this is hard work on an iPad.

would_share_with: My husband, with the overseas section and the Wedded Advisor paragraph marked, and a note asking about deposits
Back to my daughter, with the line about checking names on the certificates

cta_reaction.why: Fee in writing and quotes in AUD are what I want to see. But I would not click until my husband had read it, and I want to know it leads to a phone call with a named person, not a form that sends us sales emails. The page doesn't say what happens after I click.

top_3_changes: Break up the opening sentence so a careful but non-legal reader gets the point at once. Exact edit. OLD: In Australia, a celebrant who is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination must say the monitum in section 46(1) of the Marriage Act 1961, which opens "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law", or words to that effect, before you are married. NEW: In Australia, a civil celebrant must say a short legal statement, called the monitum, before you are married. Section 46(1) of the Marriage Act 1961 sets it out for celebrants who are not ministers of religion of a recognised denomination, and it opens "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law", or words to that effect.

Give the families a practical line about older relatives at the signing (general ceremony advice, no brand claim). Exact edit. OLD: Choose two people who will stand close by throughout, not anyone with a job to do. NEW: Choose two people who will stand close by throughout, not anyone with a job to do. If an older relative is one of them, ask your celebrant to set a chair at the signing table.

Say plainly who handles what on an overseas legal marriage, without implying the Advisor does the paperwork. Exact edit. OLD: That leaves two routes: marry under the destination's own law, or marry legally in Australia with the short script above and hold a symbolic ceremony abroad. NEW: That leaves two routes: marry under the destination's own law, or marry legally in Australia with the short script above and hold a symbolic ceremony abroad. If you marry under the destination's law, check its legal requirements with that country's authorities before you book.
